title: feat: LTE/NR Radio Bearers viewer dialog.
description:
Visualize RAN bearer connections with an interactive LCID vs time graph.
Supports LTE (positive LCID) and NR (negative LCID), with color-coded bearers
(data, signaling, SRB0).

Includes bearer tab, packet selection on click, zoom/drag controls, and
context hints (bearer ID, RLC mode).

Hi Javier,

to be completely honest (and no offense intended!) I do not find that view really useful, and it is a niche feature that 99.99% of Wireshark users will never use so I'm reluctant to having it integrated in the Wireshark core codebase. I have been in the wireless industry working on 3GPP protocols / RAN stacks in the last 26 years and I'm not understanding what's the use for this for investigation/debugging purpose. Could you please explain? I'm looking at the picture you shared on discord and still cannot imagine using it.
Moreover you are using the 3G packet-rrc.h header file (that is auto generated and that you manually modified) to add 4G/5G features which is wrong, and I do not see how it is gonna support multiple UEs.

Best regards,
Pascal.

Unfortunately, I do agree with Pascal.  I am impressed that you found your way around the codebase and made this work, but I can't think of when this would be useful for trouble-shooting.  The existing stats and graph are already quite niche, but I wouldn't want to give myself and others the burden of maintaining code that is unlikely to get used. Best regards,

Martin

Hello Pascal, Martin,

First of all, thank you for your feedback and comments, I greatly appreciate the honesty and the time you dedicated to checking my changes.

I agree this is niche and not something every Wireshark user will need. I’m working at IRISA in IMT Atlantique in France, and this was developed following a request from researcher Xavier Lagrange for pedagogical and research use. We already use custom Wireshark profiles to more easily visualize bearer lifecycle (creation/release), mainly for teaching labs where students analyze phone captures (e.g. with Accuver XCal) and try to correlate signaling with data plane behavior.

The goal is not general-purpose packet inspection, but faster interpretation of RRC-driven events during analysis sessions. In that context, having this directly in Wireshark (instead of external tooling or manual correlation) has been useful for us.

We also presented the feature to a consortium of academic and industrial partners in France, and there was some interest from people doing similar analysis/debug workflows. I understand it's still niche, but not entirely isolated.

That said, I understand the concern about adding maintenance burden to core for a limited audience.

My manager is currently on vacation and should be back next week. He’s more involved in these use cases and may be able to provide a stronger justification and possibly broader context. If possible, I’d prefer to keep this thread open until then so we can give a more complete answer.

About `packet-rrc.h`: I didn't modify the generated header directly, I modified the `-template.h`, which I understood as the source for shared/common definitions between `lte-rrc` and `nr-rrc` (I think I just didn't update/run the scripts correctly but I've re-done this locally and it looks bettter now). Since my graph supports both LTE and NR, and both rely on RRC, I placed the tap info struct there to avoid duplicating the same definition in both dissectors. If that assumption is wrong and duplication is preferred here, I can change it.

Regarding multiple UEs: I did consider it, but I don’t currently have a `.pcap` covering that case. It's something I'd add down the road.

Best regards, Javier

packet-rrc.h is not a common source for LTE and NR RRC, but the header for the UMTS RRC dissector and thus should not be impacted. If a tap is needed, then both LTE and NR dissectors should have their own one IMHO. Moreover you left aside NB-IoT that is part of LTE (like EUTRA).
While we might consider include at some point the taps in the core Wireshark (if their usefulness is proven) I really think the GUI part should not be integrated (maybe you could distribute it as a plugin?). Moreover just visualizing the bearers lifetime seems quite limited to me. For example you are not showing the RRC/NAS states, which are maybe even more important.

Best regards.

For the MAC/RLC stats, and RLC graphs, I created header files that could be shared by both generations of these protocols - see packet-rlc-3gpp-common.h and packet-mac-3gpp-common.h (these were both originally LTE only).  I haven't been working on 6G - I don't even know if these layers exist or have been defined yet..

What could be useful would be something that showed the state of the UE, and make it easy to tell things like:

* which security/integrity algorithms were negotiated?
* If bearers are suddenly released, was it because of Radio Link Failure, or was it released by RRC (if so, what cause code?) ?
* if a UE re-establishes / hands-over, showing that as one continuous callflow

That wouldn't be easy, and the level of information available probably varies a lot depending upon how the traffic is captured/collected (e.g., do you have a persistent UEId if the there is a handover?  Can you tie together MAC and RRC packets (if RRC is logged separately?)?  Do you have ciphering/integrity keys available?).

At one point (when working on LTE), I built a really comprehensive and useful GUI (I was pretty much the only user), based upon tapping our proprietary signaling protocol.  But it was really quite specialized/locked-down in terms of:

* the information we had available (in our own log file format)
* the kind of scenarios that one customer was trying to build and scale over quite a long period

I don't know how much effort it could take to make something generally useful, I didn't really contemplate it.

Hello Pascal, Martin,

Thank you again for the detailed feedback and for taking the time to explain the concerns more concretely. After revisiting the MR and discussing internally with my manager, I think I better understand both the technical and maintenance concerns.

Regarding the usefulness/justification of the feature: 4G/5G traces often observe many and frequent reconnections and disconnections, and getting a grasp of the state of the UE throughout a whole session is tricky with only the packet list.

In particular, it makes it easy to distinguish between RRC-connected and idle periods, to differentiate signaling and data bearers, and to observe how logical channels are multiplexed at the MAC layer. It also highlights situations where multiple RLC entities coexist simultaneously using different modes (e.g., RLC AM for signaling and RLC UM for other traffic), which can be difficult to understand from the packet list alone. While all of this information is technically available in the trace, correlating it mentally from individual packets is time-consuming, especially for users who are not protocol experts. The graph provides a higher-level view that makes these relationships immediately visible.

We are currently deploying laboratory sessions for Master's students where mobile network captures are analyzed as part of the coursework, and this visualization has proven useful as a teaching aid to explain bearer establishment, bearer release, protocol layering, and interactions between RRC, RLC, MAC, and the user plane. Beyond our own institution, several French academic partners involved in similar teaching and research activities have also expressed interest in the feature. While I fully agree that this is not aimed at the majority of Wireshark users, it addresses a recurring need in educational and research environments where understanding protocol behavior and resource organization is often more important than investigating individual packets.

To answer your specific points:

NB-IoT is currently not in our scope but we could study if we can get some traces. Do you have any that we could try?

About RRC/NAS states: while the graph does not explicitly display all NAS and RRC states, it already provides a visualization from which some of the main RRC state transitions can be inferred. As soon as a bearer is set up, particularly Signaling Bearer (SRB) 0, the UE is in RRC-Connected state. If the line (bearer) is interrupted or not present, it is in RRC-Idle state.

We were considering indeed showing at what point the exchanges are secured/encrypted, and with which algorithm. I can begin looking into that.

Regarding the implementation, I'd definitely move the tap structure definitions to both LTE and NR, and leave packet-rrc.h alone. Some additional information we're now looking to add to the graph is: handover visualization with a vertical line, the QoS levels, and exporting the bearer data as a CSV for further processing.

@martin.r.mathieson regarding bearer releases, I could look into that, but one can already click on the final Point of a bearer line and see the detail on the main window / packet detail.

Regarding the dependency on the capture method, we currently work with two different setups. The first is captures collected directly on a drive-test terminal, where the traffic is observed from the UE side and no persistent UE identifier is available. The second is an srsRAN setup using ZMQ, where a virtual UE identifier is available. The current implementation already works in both cases because it relies on information exposed by the existing Wireshark dissectors rather than on any proprietary log format or custom trace processing. In other words, if the traffic can be decoded by the relevant LTE/NR dissectors, the graph should be able to use that information.

For the multi-UE case specifically, I agree that the current implementation is limited. A natural next step would be to test with multiple UEs connected to srsRAN simultaneously and introduce a UE selector in the GUI to filter and visualize individual contexts.

Would all this added functionality make the feature more interesting to you? If not, I could definitely look into making the GUI a separate plugin, I think this could be a good compromise for my research team; honestly we did not consider this option before. However I'm not sure if the radio bearer info tap structure I added can also live in the / as a plugin, or if that'd have to be merged into Wireshark first? At this stage, I mainly wanted to validate whether the underlying idea/workflow could have a place in Wireshark if the implementation and scope are improved accordingly.

Best regards,

Javier

Hi Javier,

Sorry for the delay.

I do not have any NB-IoT pcap to share as to be honest I do not use Wireshark to capture over the air messages (in my company we have our own logging tool that is better suited than Wireshark for that). But givne that NB-IoT uses the same procedures as LTE, you could easily add the same code as for the EUTRA RRC messages.

Regarding the RRC/NAS state, your statement is wrong: a UE using SRB 0 is NOT in RRC connected state! It is performing a random access procedure that, if everything goes fine, will lead to the reception of a RRC setup message message that will create a SRB1 and have the UE transition from idle state to connected state. And a RRC release message will not necessarily lead to a transition to idle state as the UE could be put in inactive state.

As it is right now, the taps only have a partial coverage of all the use cases (no NB-IoT, no inactive support with release/resume messages, etc). The tap would have to be integrated in the Wireshark official source code before you can move the GUI part as a plugin. To be honest I have never written a GUI plugin myself so I'm not sure if there is any potential blocking point for your use case or not, but Roland told me it should work fine. So if you want to push this forward, the first step would be to integrate the taps in the Wireshark code base.

Best regards,
Pascal.
I’m able to provide NB-IoT traces from the nRF9151 if this is of interest. We export the packets from a standard modem trace.
